project_name: BioValue AI demo: fictional softwood kraft lignin stream
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.
1 piece(s) of input or evidence text read like instructions to the AI and were replaced before the agents saw them (see the execution trace).

constraints: The stream is currently routed to internal fuel, so diverting it to a commercial product would require changing its current use.
The mill has no lignin dryer, so buyers needing dry powder would need to provide or install drying before use.
The mill has no solvent or membrane fractionation equipment, limiting applications that require fractionated lignin.
The mill has no chemical-modification equipment, limiting applications that require modified lignin.
The stream leaves as wet filter cake at uncertain moisture, which increases shipping mass and creates handling constraints for dry-product applications.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, so pathway specifications involving these properties cannot yet be assessed.
Covered cake storage is limited to the recorded operating capacity, so storage duration and shipment scheduling may constrain diversion.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demo data, not measured mill data; all figures are illustrative assumptions and must be replaced with production records and laboratory data before decisions.
The wet quantity and moisture have recorded annual ranges, and the profile states that volume and quality are assumed to vary over the year.
The lignin analytical method is stated for illustration only and should be confirmed before comparing the composition with buyer specifications.
Moisture is marked uncertain and should be verified through ongoing cake-moisture logging.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are not measured and remain material data gaps.
agent.summary: Validated fictional softwood kraft lignin filter-cake profile: the recorded dry-matter balance and composition checks pass, with no reported inconsistencies. The stream is available as wet cake, while missing molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium data and the fictional status prevent reliable commercial qualification.

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can be used as a partial replacement for phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin has been reported as industrially proven for veneer plywood and to meet EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.

A laboratory study used depolymerized lignin for resin in which lignin supplied 50% of the phenolic component, and reported that viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in that study.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include plywood producers and manufacturers of wood-based panels that use phenol-formaldehyde or lignin-phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires an activation or depolymerization step before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A plywood adhesive application is reported against EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
The laboratory resin application assessed viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard.

limitations: The evidence combines reviews, vendor literature, and a laboratory study; the vendor performance and cost claims are not accompanied by a cited test report.
The reported depolymerized-lignin molecular-weight range is for lignin used in the process, not necessarily a delivered-mill specification.
The EN 314-2 claim concerns UPM BioPiva and does not establish qualification of the fictional stream.
The pathway generally requires activation or depolymerization, while the provided feedstock profile says the mill has no chemical-modification equipment.
missing_information: No named buyers, purchase agreements, regional demand, current lignin price, or contract terms are provided.
No evidence establishes that this wet filter cake meets a buyer's moisture, ash, molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, or sodium specifications.
No commercial throughput, delivered volume, or qualification timeline is provided for the fictional stream.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes a documented producer claim that lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is industrially proven for veneer plywood, alongside established market-scale phenolic-resin use for wood panels. It does not document several producers selling the lignin product to established buyers, so it does not reach level 5.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin can partially replace petroleum-based polyols in rigid polyurethane and polyisocyanurate foams.

Lignin can partially replace petroleum-based polyols in flexible polyurethane foam; kraft lignins were suggested as potentially suitable for heavy-duty foams because they produced denser, stiffer foams.
The evidence covers polyurethane foams, panels, coatings, and rubber-replacement uses, but rates lignin-based polyurethane uses at TRL 6 overall rather than for a specific kraft-lignin product.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include rigid insulation-foam producers and other manufacturers of rigid polyurethane or polyisocyanurate products.
Potential customers include flexible-foam producers, including manufacturers serving automotive and heavy-duty foam applications.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol.

qualification_requirements.statement: For rigid polyurethane foam, total lignin hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups, is cited as an acceptable range.
In one study, rigid foams with 30 wt% unmodified lignin replacing petroleum-based polyol were assessed against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Kraft lignin generally needs significant treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies, and the cited TRL 6 applies to a broad polyurethane row rather than specifically to kraft-lignin foam.
Results vary by lignin type; the best performer in one study was enzymatic hydrolysis lignin, while kraft lignins showed failures or reduced performance in some tests.
The flexible-foam study identified sulfur odor as a known drawback of some softwood kraft lignins but did not measure odor.
A review identifying commercialization barriers was available only as an abstract.
missing_information: No named buyers, commercial sales, purchase agreements, regional demand, current lignin price, or contract terms are provided.
No evidence establishes that the fictional wet cake has the required total hydroxyl value, moisture, viscosity, solubility, or odor performance.
No pilot-scale qualification, commercial production volume, or customer validation is documented for this stream.
The mill lacks chemical-modification equipment, but the evidence does not quantify the cost or practical route for an external modification step.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows research testing of lignin-containing polyurethane foams and a broad technology-readiness assessment, but it does not document commercial sales, named buyers, or an industry development partnership for lignin-based polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#2: The precursor accounts for about 50% of carbon fiber manufacturing cost.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.

applications.statement: Softwood lignin can serve as a carbon-fiber precursor, although the evidence reports that it is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent.

Lignin-derived hard carbon is an application for sodium-ion battery anodes, and kraft-lignin hard carbon carbonized at 1,200 °C has been compared favorably with sulfonated-lignin hard carbon on initial coulombic efficiency.
Lignin can be converted to activated carbon, including when the precursor is too impure for other carbon-material applications.

target_customers.statement: Potential customers include carbon-fiber producers and industrial users of carbon fiber, including automotive applications.
Potential customers include sodium-ion battery-anode manufacturers and battery manufacturers or carmakers involved in qualifying anode materials.
Potential customers include activated-carbon producers and users of activated carbon.

competing_materials.statement: The named incumbent for carbon fiber is PAN-based carbon fiber.
The named competing hard-carbon feedstocks include fossil precursors such as anthracite or pitch.
Conventional activated carbon is the competing material for the activated-carbon application.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specification requires lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
Kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber needed purification, and softwood lignin needs a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation in the cited study, although lower ash improves yield.
Qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years according to the cited company material.

limitations: Carbon fiber, hard carbon, and activated carbon have substantially different quality requirements; carbon-fiber specifications should not be generalized to the other two applications.
The carbon-fiber specifications are cited secondhand and come from a study using lignin from a near-neutral hemicellulose extraction process rather than standard kraft pulping.
The hard-carbon feedstock comparison is a review, and the activated-carbon result is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
The battery qualification timing and pilot information are company material and include forward-looking or time-specific statements.
The provided feedstock has missing sodium, molecular-weight, and other analytical data, and is available as wet filter cake rather than a characterized dry precursor.
missing_information: No named buyers, purchase agreements, regional demand, current delivered price, contract terms, or confirmed offtake are provided.
No evidence establishes that the fictional stream meets carbon-fiber precursor limits for ash, volatiles, particulates, or residual carbohydrates.
No evidence provides a product specification, cell-performance target, or qualification result for hard carbon made from this stream.
No evidence provides activated-carbon surface-area, pore-volume, yield, or end-user performance data for this stream.
No commercial throughput, processing yield, drying cost, or scale-up plan is provided for the fictional stream.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially relevant carbon-fiber precursor project at TRL 5, a battery-material pilot announcement, and a stated battery/carmaker qualification process. These are pilots and development evidence rather than documented commercial sales by several lignin producers, so the evidence aligns with level 3.

processing_requirements.statement: The kraft lignin would need activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins.
A commercial route would also require handling the wet filter cake and providing drying or an equivalent buyer-side preparation step because the mill has no lignin dryer.

adoption_barriers.statement: The mill lacks chemical-modification equipment, while this pathway generally requires activation or depolymerization.
The stream has not been shown to meet buyer requirements for moisture, ash, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, or sodium.
Although industrially proven performance is reported for veneer plywood, that evidence does not qualify this fictional stream or establish a buyer, offtake, or commercial qualification route.
Diversion would displace the stream's current internal-fuel use and would require suitable logistics for wet cake, limited covered storage, and shipment scheduling.

uncertainties: TRL 5 and the compatibility score relate principally to the cited carbon-fiber precursor evidence; the other carbon-material applications have different requirements.

The missing sodium, molecular-weight, and other analytical data, together with uncertain moisture, limit precursor qualification.

A demonstrated low-cost route that avoids major new assets or uses an external partner could improve commercialization feasibility, particularly for phenolic resins and polyurethanes.

caveats: The feedstock profile is explicitly fictional, so all operational, qualification, and economic conclusions require confirmation on the actual mill stream.

report.summary: The deterministic engine ranks carbon_materials first at attractiveness 2.19, with a range from 1.95 to 2.75, because it is the only pathway with enough assessed weight to rank. Its strongest supports are TRL 5 development evidence and pilot or qualification market evidence; its main weakness is score 1 feedstock compatibility for the checked carbon-fiber requirements and score 2 commercialization feasibility. Phenolic resins and polyurethanes are not ranked because too much criterion weight remains unassessed. Phenolic resins has the best market evidence, while polyurethane has broad technical-readiness evidence, but both require feedstock testing and economics before a reliable comparison is possible.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
The precursor accounts for about 50% of carbon fiber manufacturing cost.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
